Diameters And Chords

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: This is a picture, not a game: lines cross a circle in a pattern that links two pairs of points.
How to play: Drag the round points, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick a box to show names or a hint, or press Reset to start again.
Look for the math

Move the six points around the circle and watch what happens to the two yellow K points. The picture is set up so that two pairs of points either both meet or both stay apart. That is not an accident.

What the picture builds

The centre O is marked. Each of BBt, CCt and MtNt goes straight through O, so each is a diameter of the circle: its ends are opposite each other. The chords BAb and CAc cross the third diameter at M and N. Then Kb is the other point where the line NBt meets the circle, and Kc comes from MCt. Dragging either end of MtNt keeps the two ends opposite, just as in the old applet.

The claim, and why it is true

The page asks us to prove an if and only if: Ab = Ac exactly when Kb = Kc. Suppose first that the two A points have merged into one point A. Look at the six points A, B, Bt, Kb, Ct, C around the circle. In this hexagon, opposite sides meet at N (from AC and BtKb), at O (from BBt and CtC) and at some point M′ (from AB and KbCt).

By Pascal's theorem those three meeting points lie on one line. Two of them, N and O, lie on the diameter MtNt, so M′ lies on that diameter too. But M is where AB crosses that same diameter, so M′ = M. The line MCt is therefore the line KbCt, which is exactly how Kc was made. Hence Kc = Kb.

The other way, and what the checks found

The two roles can be swapped: start from a single K point, rebuild the two lines through it and read off the two A points. The same hexagon argument then forces Ab = Ac. The logic test does this in both directions on thousands of generated pictures and also compares every computed point with a second, independent transcription of the applet's own method. The claim holds whenever B, C and Mt are distinct points. One caveat: the old applet calls the A points "together" when they are less than one pixel apart, and if B and C are themselves almost on top of each other, the two K points can be under a pixel apart for that trivial reason while the A points are far apart. The exact statement is unaffected.

The old page embeds two copies of the Java applet, one with the names and hints switched off and one with them on; browsers no longer run that plug-in, so the picture here follows the applet's bytecode and the page's written solution. The old "hint" checkbox had an empty drawing method; here it highlights the Pascal hexagon instead. That is the one deliberate change.

Try dragging Ac onto Ab with the arrow keys: watch the two yellow K points merge at the same moment.
